extraction.name: Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research
extraction.description: We present the Natural Questions corpus, a question answering data set. Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present.
extraction.creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, T., Palomaki, J., Redfield, O., Collins, M., Parikh, A., Alberti, C., Epstein, D., Polosukhin, I., Devlin, J., Lee, K., Toutanova, K., Jones, L., Kelcey, M., Chang, M., Dai, A. M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7, 453-466.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream. Annotators are presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Queries from Google search engine; Wikipedia pages from top 5 search results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are filtered using heuristics to discard non-questions. Only queries of 8 words or more that match specific patterns are kept. Questions are run through Google search engine and only those with a Wikipedia page in top 5 results are retained.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators are presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair. They first determine if the question is good (fact-seeking). For good questions, they select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) that contains enough information to answer the question (long answer). If no such box exists, they mark null. For examples with a long answer, they select the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question (short answer), or flag yes/no/null.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-hoc evaluation of annotation quality using expert judgments (four experts) and 25-way annotations on 302 examples to study human variability. Precision of long answers is 90%, short answers 84%. Variability analysis shows that for many questions there is genuine ambiguity; annotators disagree on whether an answer exists and on the location of the best answer.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for training (307,373 examples), 5 for development (7,830 examples) and test (7,842 examples), 25 for a subset of 302 examples
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Like any data set there may be biases in the choice of Wikipedia as the source of evidence documents.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on longer queries (8 words or more) and Wikipedia pages; future work may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or other domains. There is variability in annotations due to genuine ambiguity.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and test data for question answering systems. The task is to output a long answer (paragraph or null) and a short answer (entity/entities or null) given a question and a Wikipedia page.
